title: Why algorithms matter: Knuth 1968, Dijkstra in a cafe 1956
story:
Dijkstra told this story himself, in a 2001 interview, and the details are better than the paraphrase usually given.

The lab wanted a problem that non-mathematicians could understand, for a demonstration. The question chosen was what the shortest way is to travel from Rotterdam to Groningen — or in general, from one given city to another. He designed the algorithm in about twenty minutes, sitting on a cafe terrace in Amsterdam with his young fiancée while out shopping, without pencil and paper. And he attributed its simplicity to exactly that: one of the reasons it is so nice, he said, is that he designed it without pencil and paper.

That last remark is the part worth carrying. A constraint that looks like a handicap — no notation, no scratch work, nothing to lean on — forced a solution simple enough to be held in a head, and the simplicity is why it survived. It was published three years later, in 1959, as a note on two problems in connexion with graphs.

The complementary half arrived in 1968, when Donald Knuth published the first volume of The Art of Computer Programming, establishing the analysis of algorithms as a discipline: a program's resource consumption derived mathematically rather than measured after the fact.

The reason that matters is not rigour for its own sake. Measuring tells you what one input cost on one machine. Deriving tells you how the cost grows, and growth is the only thing that settles what happens at sizes you have not tried — which is every size that matters, because the ones you tried are the ones that already worked.

Put numbers on it. A procedure whose work grows with the square of the input, run on a million items, needs on the order of a million million operations. One whose work grows as the input times its logarithm needs around twenty million. That is not a difference in speed; it is the difference between a program that finishes and a program that does not, and no hardware closes it. Hardware buys constant factors. The growth rate is what decides whether constant factors are worth anything.

Now the correction that matters more than the principle, because the principle is usually taught without it. Growth rates deliberately ignore constants, and constants are not small. An insertion sort, quadratic in the worst case, beats a sort that grows as the input times its logarithm on small inputs and on nearly-sorted ones — it has tiny per-element overhead, no recursion, and it walks memory in the order the hardware prefers. Which is why real sorting implementations are hybrids: a good asymptotic algorithm for the large partitions, switching to the quadratic one below a threshold of a few dozen elements.

So the honest statement is narrower than the slogan. The asymptotically better algorithm wins for all sufficiently large inputs, and sufficiently large is doing real work in that sentence — for some pairs of algorithms the crossover is beyond any input you will ever see, and then the worse one is simply the right choice. Asymptotic analysis tells you which algorithm eventually wins; it does not tell you whether you will ever get there.

What the two contributions leave you with is a pair of habits rather than a body of facts. Derive the growth rate before writing the thing, because it is cheap to do and it decides the outcome at sizes you cannot test. And keep the solution small enough to hold in your head, on the grounds that the best-known algorithm in this field was produced in twenty minutes by someone who had nothing to write with.

problem.shape: A procedure works on the inputs it was tried with, and will meet larger ones.

cost.time: deriving the growth takes thought before any code exists, at a point where the problem is least well understood

worked.problem: When would a quadratic sort such as insertion sort outperform one that grows as the input times its logarithm?
worked.reasoning:
On small inputs and on nearly-ordered ones — and the reason is that asymptotic analysis deliberately discards exactly the thing that decides the answer at those sizes.

The growth class describes how cost scales, not what it is. Insertion sort's per-element work is tiny: a comparison and a shift, no recursion, no partitioning, no auxiliary allocation, and it walks memory in the order the hardware prefers, so its cache behaviour is close to ideal. A sort in the better class pays for its scaling with partitioning or merging overhead, recursive call management, and often extra memory. Below some input size that overhead exceeds the difference the growth rate makes.

That size is the crossover point, and it is a property of the pair of implementations rather than of the classes. In practice for sorting it falls somewhere in the range of a few dozen elements — which is why real implementations are hybrids, using a good asymptotic algorithm for the large partitions and switching to insertion sort below a threshold.

Nearly-ordered input is the second case and it is a different argument. Insertion sort's cost depends on how far elements must move, so on input that is already close to sorted it approaches linear time — better than the better class, not merely competitive with it. Real-world data is very often nearly ordered, which is why algorithms that detect and exploit existing runs do well on it.

The general principle is still right and worth stating precisely rather than as a slogan: the asymptotically better algorithm wins for all sufficiently large inputs, and no constant-factor improvement changes a growth rate. On a million items, quadratic growth means on the order of a million million operations while the better class means around twenty million — the difference between finishing and not finishing, and no hardware closes it.

But 'sufficiently large' is carrying real weight in that sentence. For some pairs of algorithms the crossover is beyond any input that will ever be presented, and then the asymptotically worse one is simply correct. So the discipline is to derive the growth rate and then check it against the sizes that actually occur, rather than treating the class as the answer.

Which is the honest summary of what asymptotic analysis does: it tells you which algorithm eventually wins. It does not tell you whether you will ever get there.

problem.practice: Take a procedure you have only ever run on small inputs and derive how its work grows. Then compute what that means at a hundred times the size, and decide whether you have a program or a demonstration.

beats.broke: A procedure that worked on a handful of items was assumed to work on many, because nothing about testing it at small size reveals how its cost grows.
beats.fix: Derive how the work grows with the input rather than timing one input, since the growth rate decides the outcome at every size the measurement did not cover.
beats.cost: Growth rates discard the constants, so the asymptotically better algorithm can lose at every size that actually occurs — which is why production sorts switch to a quadratic algorithm below a few dozen elements.

interview.trap: Answering that the better class always wins at scale and leaving it there. The question is about where the crossover is, and for some pairs of algorithms it lies beyond any input that will ever be presented.
